title: Strengthening Public Health Preparedness through Integrated Biomedical Strategies
author: Goshen David Miteu
excerpt: Vaccines, antivirals and monoclonal antibodies are not competitors. A 2025 paper in Discover Public Health shows how they form a layered defence against infectious disease.
body:
At RAISSAT, we are committed to strengthening public health systems through applied research, innovation, and collaboration. Our mission recognizes that sustainable global health security depends on both discovery and the **integration of science, policy, and practice.** Building resilient health systems requires a proactive approach; one that unites disease prevention, rapid response, and equitable access to biomedical tools. In this spirit, we draw inspiration from a recent publication titled “Understanding the Public Health Value of Vaccines, Antivirals, and Monoclonal Antibodies as Complementary Strategies Against Infectious Diseases”, published by Springer Nature on October 30th, 2025. It offers a timely reflection on how modern biomedical countermeasures can synergize to protect populations from viral threats.

The study, authored by **Goshen David Miteu**, explores why vaccines, antivirals, and monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) should not be viewed as competitors but as complementary public health tools that form a layered, resilient defense against infectious diseases. Miteu discusses critical questions: Why are certain pathogens targeted with multiple interventions while others are not? Should resources be distributed evenly across all three? And how can these strategies co-exist efficiently in pandemic preparedness planning?

Drawing on real case scenarios from **measles** and **Ebola** to **COVID-19**, the paper demonstrates how each intervention addresses unique phases of disease prevention and control. Vaccines act as the first line of defense; antivirals reduce viral replication and disease severity; and mAbs provide targeted, rapid protection, especially for vulnerable populations. Rather than redundancy, this synergy ensures that public health systems remain adaptable and future-ready.

This work mirrors our ongoing commitment at RAISSAT. We exist to close the global gap between discovery and deployment. From evidence to impact, in another sense. Some examples of how we do this are by advocating for evidence-based policies, One Health integration, and **global collaboration** to strengthen pandemic resilience. Innovative thinking within biomedical and biological sciences is one way we achieve RAISSAT’s vision in public health: to transform research into sustainable, life-saving impact.
